name: Shanghai dialect / Shanghainese
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 3 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Hashimoto, Mantaro J. 1971. A guide to the Shanghai dialect. Princeton, NJ: Princeton University, Chinese Linguistics Project. (ERIC microfiche scan, archive.org)
catalog_locator: Chapter 2 'Phonological Description', sec. 2.4 'Tones' and sec. 2.5 'Tone Change', pp. 11-12 (microfiche frames 16-17)
catalog_quote: Phonetically Shanghai has seven tones, yin-p'ing, yang-p'ing, yin-shang, yin-ch'ü, yang-ch'ü, yin-ju and yang-ju. ... The phonological representation of Shanghai morphemes thus requires only four tones, namely p'ing, shang, ch'ü and ju. ... 2.5 Tone Change. The most conspicuous tone change in Shainghai [sic] is that of the yang-p'ing and the yang-ch'ü. The low rising pitch-contour of the yang-p'ing (which we indicate as 12) and the high rising pitch-contour of the yang-ch'ü (15) change into high falling unless the syllable carries primary stress. Shanghai composite nouns normally carry primary stress on their first syllables. Hence the following can be observed: zaŋ12-tʃĩn53 'the nerves': tʃĩn53-zaŋ42 'spirits' ...
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Wu Chinese (wuch1236) is not in the catalog. this search of works with stress in the title had two title hits: Lyu 2018 (UW-Madison dissertation on Ningbo prosodic phonology, 457 pp.) and Selkirk & Shen 1990 (Prosodic domains in Shanghai Chinese, in Inkelas & Zec eds.). Neither text was obtainable: Lyu 2018 is ProQuest-only (not in MINDS@UW; only a one-sentence Google Books description and the abstract/reference list of the derived article Lyu 2019, IJCHL 6(1):119-161, doi:10.1075/ijchl.19004.lyu, were readable — both are about the tone-sandhi domain = prosodic word, silent on stress placement); Selkirk & Shen 1990 exists only as an access-restricted Internet Archive lending scan (phonologysyntaxc0000unse) and a Google Books partial preview (qt0f6KuNXmkC), neither readable by automated download, and it is not on the authors' homepages. Both items are 'unclear' for word stress (prosodic-domain/tone-sandhi studies of Wu varieties), both 'no-catalog-record', priority medium. As a lead outside the item list, Duanmu 1999 (JEAL 8:1-38, doi:10.1023/A:1008353028173, paywalled; abstract saved) treats Shanghai as a moraic-/disyllabic-trochee system where 'the initial syllable determines the tonal pattern of a multisyllabic domain' — the likeliest first-hand stress source for Shanghai Wu, but no page-located stress statement was read, so no new stress statement was found.org metadata and publisher pages.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Wu is a tone language (Shanghai: five citation tones, four phonological). Within a compound (the tone-sandhi domain) primary stress falls on the first syllable; only the stressed initial syllable keeps its underlying tone, and the non-initial syllables lose their own tones (Hashimoto's 'high falling' replacement; in Chen & Gussenhoven 2015 the initial tone determines the f0 contour of the whole tone unit). This is the left-headed (initial) stress account of Northern Wu formalised by Duanmu 1993/1995 and Chen 2000 (both paywalled) and restated by Wen 2026: 3.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned by Hashimoto. Edkins 1868: 18 notes 'a secondary accent on some other syllable in groups of three' (19th-century description; accent there said to prefer the last syllable).
new_statements.exceptions: Hashimoto: 'normally' - no explicit exception list. Contradicting/complicating evidence from the same language: Zhang 2006 (Shaoxing) says Shaoxing is right-prominent with an iambic stress foot (rightmost syllable of the foot is the head; trochaic only when the second syllable is an unstressed suffix such as the adjective marker [go?]); Wen 2026 finds no independent acoustic correlate of stress in Shaoxing and argues stress is inferred circularly from tone-sandhi dominance. Stress in Wu is therefore a phonological construct read off tone-sandhi patterns rather than an independently measured prominence.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the compound / tone-sandhi unit (polysyllabic word), not the phrase; monosyllabic words keep their citation tone. Left-dominant (initial) pattern is for Shanghai and the Taihu (Northern Wu) group generally; Southern Wu (e.g. Wenzhou) is right-dominant, and Shaoxing (Lin-Shao) is analysed as right-prominent by Zhang 2006. Chen & Gussenhoven 2015 note the lack of phrasal-level prominence as an open question.
new_statements.identity_note: Deciding quote describes the Shanghai dialect (Shanghainese, Glottolog shan1293, Taihu/Su-Hu-Jia group of Wu). The two other first-hand open sources (Zhang 2006, Wen 2026) describe Shaoxing (Glottolog Lin-Shao, lins1238; Zhang calls it 'southern Wu' but Glottolog places it in Taihu/Northern Wu) and give a different picture (right-prominent per Zhang; no independent evidence for stress per Wen). Wu is a dialect continuum; no single stress statement covers wuch1236 as a whole.

tone_statements.citation: Yan, Hanbo, Yu-Fu Chien & Jie Zhang. 2021. The representation of variable tone sandhi patterns in Shanghai Wu. Laboratory Phonology 12(1).
tone_statements.quote: Five citation tones are identified in the New varieties of Shanghai. … Tl is described as high falling from either high [5] or mid-high [4] down to a variable offset … T2 is described as high rising … T3 is described as low rising … T4 is described as short high at [5] or [4]. … TS is described as short low rising … Tl to T3 are Long while T4 and TS Short in terms of Truncation. Tl, T2, and T4 are Upper Register while T3 and TS are Lower Register. Tl is falling towards a Lo-terminal-target, while the other four are ascending towards a Hi-terminal-target.
tone_statements.locator: pp. 22-24, sec. 2.2.3 'Tones' (Chapter 2, Shanghai Phonology), with Table 2.04 and Fig. 2.02; phonological features restated Table 9.01, p. 222
tone_statements.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
tone_statements.summary: Five citation tones on every syllable, cross-classified by register (upper/lower), length (long/short) and contour: T1 falling, T2-T5 rising; eight allotones; compound stress set by the first tone.

tone_statements.citation: Shi, Menghui, Yiya Chen & Maarten Mous. 2020. Tonal split and laryngeal contrast of onset consonant in Lili Wu Chinese. Journal of the Acoustical Society of America 147(4): 2901-2916.
tone_statements.quote: The tone sandhi pattern in Shanghai Wu is unique in that it simultaneously embodies tonally and positionally induced sandhi and that the sandhi pattern is structure-dependent. The tonal inventory of Shanghai is given in Figure 1. Tones 1 (51), 2 (35), and 3 (24) occur on unchecked syllables, while Tones 4 (44) and 5 (12) occur on checked (/-closed) syllables. Disyllabic sequences in Shanghai undergo different types of tone sandhi depending on their syntactic structure. For instance, modifier-noun compounds spread the initial tone across the entire word (left-dominant sandhi) …
tone_statements.locator: p. 1, sec. 1 Introduction (with Figure 1 'Shanghai tonal inventory' and Table 1 'Left- and right-dominant sandhis in Shanghai')
tone_statements.summary: Five lexical tones: 51, 35, 24 on unchecked syllables, 44 and 12 on checked syllables; disyllables take left-dominant (spreading) or right-dominant sandhi by syntactic structure; f0 data, 48 speakers.

tone_statements.citation: Takahashi, Yasunori (2019). The phonological status of Low tones in Shanghai tone sandhi. Language and Linguistics 20. John Benjamins Publishing Company. pp. 15-45.
tone_statements.quote: In Zhenhai, any citation monosyllable or monosyllabic word belongs to one of six contrasting tones. … Tone 1: High falling pitch with short initial level component … Tone 2: Concave pitch in the mid pitch range terminated by a glottal stop … Tone 3: Convex pitch in the low-mid pitch range … Tone 4: Low rising pitch with either a level or slightly falling initial component and glottal stop offset … Tone 5: Very short high level or falling pitch with glottal stop offset … Tone 6: Very short low rising pitch with glottal stop offset
tone_statements.summary: Zhenhai Wu (Ningbo area, not Shanghai city): six citation tones (high falling, mid concave, low convex, low rising, two short checked) on every syllable; word stress interacts with tone in sandhi.

tone_statements.citation: Gao, Jiayin & Pierre A. Hallé. 2017. Phonetic and phonological properties of tones in Shanghai Chinese. Cahiers de Linguistique Asie Orientale 46(1): 1-31.
tone_statements.quote: There are eight lexical tones in Lili Wu Chinese. … T1 is a high-register level tone (h-level) while T2 is a low-register rising tone (l-rising). T3 starts within the high register and falls (h-falling). T4 is a low-register level tone (l-level). T5 has a convex contour which starts within the high register, falls and ends with a slight rise (h-dipping). T6 is realized with a similar f0 contour to that of T5 but starts within the low register (l-dipping). … T7 … sounds like a high-register level tone (short-h-level). T8 is a low-register level tone (short-l-level).
tone_statements.locator: p. 2902, sec. I.A 'Wu Chinese and tonal split with aspiration onsets in Lili Wu', with Table I (tone values 44, 13, 53, 22, 423, 213, 5, 3) and Fig. 1
tone_statements.summary: Lili Wu (Wujiang, Suzhou), a Northern Wu dialect: eight lexical tones in high/low registers by onset voicing (44, 13, 53, 22, 423, 213, short 5, 3); aspirated onsets lower Shang/Qu/Ru tones.

tone_statements.citation: Gao, Jiayin. 2015. Interdependence between Tones, Segments, and Phonation Types in Shanghai Chinese: Acoustics, Articulation, Perception, and Evolution [Interdépendance entre tons, segments et types de phonation en shanghaïen]. Thèse de doctorat (Phonétique), Sorbonne Paris Cité (Université Sorbonne Nouvelle - Paris 3), defended 21 May 2015.
tone_statements.quote: On monosyllabic words, and characters read out in citation form, Lishui has seven tones. … There are two tones ending in a glottal stop and five without. Of these unstopped tones, all have contour pitch shapes, and three are complex as well: high falling, convex (or rising-falling), dipping, mid falling-level, and low falling-level. The stopped tones also differ in pitch height and contour: a high stopped tone and a low rising stopped tone. … Although the falling-level tones have a level component to them, none of the citation tones are level.
tone_statements.locator: pp. 87-88, sec. 6.2 Auditory Description (table 6.1 p. 88); tone values also in Abstract p. iii and Table 6.15 p. 111 / Table 9.2 p. 190
tone_statements.summary: Lishui (southern Wu): seven citation tones, dipping 324, falling-level 433 and 211, falling 52, convex 342, stopped 5 and 23; only short high [5] is level; right-focussed sandhi; stress not described.

tone_statements.citation: Steed, William James. 2010. Lishui Wu tone and tone sandhi: an acoustically-based description. PhD thesis, Australian National University. hdl 1885/150520.
tone_statements.quote: These surveys found that SHUD had five tones (T3=T5, T2=T4=T6), Bǎoshān had six tones (T3=T5, T4=T6), Nánhuì had seven tones (T4=T6) and Sōngjiāng had eight tones … SHUD finished the merger of T2, T4 and T6 and further merged T3 and T5 in the Yīn register. … It can be seen from Figure 6.1 that old and young people have completely merged T2, T4 and T6 into /13/. … As seen from Table 6.4, none of the three indexes is significant, so the merger of T2, T4 and T6 of SHUD is confirmed in my dataset.
tone_statements.locator: p. 35, sec. 2.4.2.1 'The development of citation tone' (five-tone count; values in Table 2.5, p. 37: SHUD T1 53, T5 34, T6 23, T7 55, T8 12) and pp. 188-189, sec. 6.1.2 'Shànghǎi urban dialect (SHUD)'
tone_statements.summary: Shanghai urban: eight Middle Chinese categories merged to five citation tones (53, 34, low rising 23~13, checked 55, 12); F0 of 20 urban speakers confirms the T2/T4/T6 merger; left-dominant sandhi.

tone_statements.citation: Shunde, Jin (1997). Toward a systematic account of Shanghai tonal phonology. In Studies in Chinese Phonology. De Gruyter. pp. 125-156.
tone_statements.quote: Shanghai Chinese has five lexical tones, including three unchecked tones and two checked tones. The checked tones are carried by syllables ending with a glottal stop. … In our work, we follow Xu and Tang’s (1988) notation for Shanghai tones, and thus note T1 as 53, T2 as 34, T3 as 23, T4 as 55, and T5 as 12. … the stress pattern in these dialects are often refered to as a “heavy-light” pattern (Ballard, 1989: 105). More specifically, at the word/compound level, the stress is assigned leftmostly (Chen, 2000: 309).
tone_statements.locator: p. 19 (sec. 2.1.3 Tone), p. 21 (sec. 2.1.3.1 Citation tones) and p. 26 (sec. 2.1.3.2 Tone sandhi and stress)
tone_statements.summary: Five lexical tones on the syllable: T1 53, T2 34, T3 23 (unchecked), T4 55, T5 12 (checked, glottal-stop final); yin/yang register tied to onset voicing; left-dominant sandhi; word stress leftmost.

tone_statements.citation: Rose, Phil. 1993. A linguistic-phonetic acoustic analysis of Shanghai tones. Australian Journal of Linguistics 13(2): 185-220.
tone_statements.quote: In Shanghai Wu, diachronically, Yinshang and Yinqu merged into one tone Yinqu, and Yangping, Yangshang, and Yangqu merged into one tone, Yangqu. Therefore, there are five tones in modern Shanghai. T1 represents Yinping, T2 represents Yinqu … T4 represents Yinru, and T5 represents Yangru. T1 to T3 occur on open or sonorant-closed syllables, and T4 and T5 occur on checked syllables, which are syllables closed by a glottal stop, as shown in (6). … (6) Shanghai tones Tone 1 53 Tone 2 24 Tone 3 13 Tone 4 55 Tone 5 13
tone_statements.locator: pp. 14-15, sec. 2.1 'Shanghai tone sandhi patterns', example (6)
tone_statements.summary: Five citation tones on the syllable: 53, 24, 13 on open/sonorant-final syllables, 55 and 13 on checked syllables; compounds take left-dominant sandhi (first tone spreads), phrases right-dominant.

tone_statements.citation: Cao, Jianfen & Ian Maddieson. 1992. An exploration of phonation types in Wu dialects of Chinese. Journal of Phonetics 20(1): 77-92.
tone_statements.quote: Shanghat is traditionally described as contrasting five tones on citation monosyllables or monosyllabic words. … Of the five pairs of comparable tones in the two dialects (falling, mid concave, low dipping, high short, low short), the falling pair was found to differ in offset and contour. … This is shown by the fact that Shanghai, with five tones, has the same degree of clustering as Zhenhai, or North Vietnamese, with six. … Shanghai only needs one distinctive tone feature, to handle the contrast between tones | and 2: [+/- Fail]. All other features of the five tones are predictable.
tone_statements.locator: p. 186 (sec. 2 Auditory transcriptions of Shanghai tones), p. 217 and p. 218 (sec. 5 discussion)
tone_statements.summary: Five citation tones on monosyllables: high falling, mid concave (rising), low dipping (rising), high short, low short rising; F0/duration of 16 speakers; only tones 1 vs 2 need a feature [+/-Fall].

tone_statements.citation: Rose, Phil. 1990. Acoustics and Phonology of Complex Tone Sandhi. Phonetica 47(1-2): 1-35.
tone_statements.quote: Syllables in Shanghai can be non-checked (open or sonorant-closed) or checked (closed by a glottal stop [ʔ]), with tones 53, 24, and 13 occurring on the former and tones 55 and 13 occurring on the latter.1 … High register tones, tones 53, 24, and 55, only occur in syllables beginning with voiceless consonants (the historical yin tones), and low register tones, tones 13 and 13, only occur in those starting with voiced ones (the historical yang tones).
tone_statements.locator: p. 2 (Art. 15, page 2 of 24), sec. 1.1 'Tone sandhi in Shanghai Wu'
tone_statements.summary: Five tones (Chao numbers): 53, 24, 13 on non-checked syllables, 55 and 13 on checked; high-register tones need voiceless onsets, low voiced; disyllables show rightward tone extension or reduction.

sources.citation: Wen, Xinyi. 2026. Phantom stress in tone sandhi: evidence from Shaoxing Wu Chinese. Amsterdam: LOT (LOT 724; Leiden PhD, defended). 183 pp.
sources.note: pp. 2-3: 'Shanghai Wu is regarded as having left-headed word stress; the unstressed (i.e., non-initial) syllables undergo tonal deletion, while the underlying tone of the stressed syllable is preserved.. (e.g., M. Y. Chen, 2000; Duanmu, 1993, 1995)'. Sec. 5.2.1 pp. 110-111 (Shaoxing): 'we found no independent acoustic correlates of stress beyond tonal patterns themselves' (duration of disyllables: final syllable consistently longer regardless of sandhi type); 'our findings reveal no such independent evidence for stress in Shaoxing Wu'.

sources.citation: Edkins, Joseph. 1868 [1853]. A grammar of colloquial Chinese, as exhibited in the Shanghai dialect. 2nd ed. Shanghai: Presbyterian Mission Press.
sources.note: Part I sec. 3 'Shanghai tones', pp. 16-18 (scanned): tables of tone combinations give 'Place of the Accent' (ult./pen./ant.) word by word; 'Obs. ii. The accent often varies between the first and the last syllable. In regard to position, it is the latter that should receive it' (p. 17); 'Obs. iii. In regard to position the accent prefers the last syllable' and a note on secondary accent in trisyllables (p. 18). 19th-century missionary description; accent interacts with tone.

sources.quote: On monosyllabic words, and characters read out in citation form, Lishui has seven tones. … There are two tones ending in a glottal stop and five without. Of these unstopped tones, all have contour pitch shapes, and three are complex as well: high falling, convex (or rising-falling), dipping, mid falling-level, and low falling-level. The stopped tones also differ in pitch height and contour: a high stopped tone and a low rising stopped tone. … Although the falling-level tones have a level component to them, none of the citation tones are level.

sources.quote: In Shanghai Wu, diachronically, Yinshang and Yinqu merged into one tone Yinqu, and Yangping, Yangshang, and Yangqu merged into one tone, Yangqu. Therefore, there are five tones in modern Shanghai. T1 represents Yinping, T2 represents Yinqu … T4 represents Yinru, and T5 represents Yangru. T1 to T3 occur on open or sonorant-closed syllables, and T4 and T5 occur on checked syllables, which are syllables closed by a glottal stop, as shown in (6). … (6) Shanghai tones Tone 1 53 Tone 2 24 Tone 3 13 Tone 4 55 Tone 5 13
sources.locator: pp. 14-15, sec. 2.1 'Shanghai tone sandhi patterns', example (6)
sources.note: Five citation tones on the syllable: 53, 24, 13 on open/sonorant-final syllables, 55 and 13 on checked syllables; compounds take left-dominant sandhi (first tone spreads), phrases right-dominant.

sources.quote: Shanghat is traditionally described as contrasting five tones on citation monosyllables or monosyllabic words. … Of the five pairs of comparable tones in the two dialects (falling, mid concave, low dipping, high short, low short), the falling pair was found to differ in offset and contour. … This is shown by the fact that Shanghai, with five tones, has the same degree of clustering as Zhenhai, or North Vietnamese, with six. … Shanghai only needs one distinctive tone feature, to handle the contrast between tones | and 2: [+/- Fail]. All other features of the five tones are predictable.
sources.locator: p. 186 (sec. 2 Auditory transcriptions of Shanghai tones), p. 217 and p. 218 (sec. 5 discussion)
sources.note: Five citation tones on monosyllables: high falling, mid concave (rising), low dipping (rising), high short, low short rising; F0/duration of 16 speakers; only tones 1 vs 2 need a feature [+/-Fall].

sources.quote: Syllables in Shanghai can be non-checked (open or sonorant-closed) or checked (closed by a glottal stop [ʔ]), with tones 53, 24, and 13 occurring on the former and tones 55 and 13 occurring on the latter.1 … High register tones, tones 53, 24, and 55, only occur in syllables beginning with voiceless consonants (the historical yin tones), and low register tones, tones 13 and 13, only occur in those starting with voiced ones (the historical yang tones).

tone.quote: In Zhenhai, any citation monosyllable or monosyllabic word belongs to one of six contrasting tones. … Tone 1: High falling pitch with short initial level component … Tone 2: Concave pitch in the mid pitch range terminated by a glottal stop … Tone 3: Convex pitch in the low-mid pitch range … Tone 4: Low rising pitch with either a level or slightly falling initial component and glottal stop offset … Tone 5: Very short high level or falling pitch with glottal stop offset … Tone 6: Very short low rising pitch with glottal stop offset

tone.quote: Shanghai Chinese has five lexical tones, including three unchecked tones and two checked tones. The checked tones are carried by syllables ending with a glottal stop. … In our work, we follow Xu and Tang’s (1988) notation for Shanghai tones, and thus note T1 as 53, T2 as 34, T3 as 23, T4 as 55, and T5 as 12. … the stress pattern in these dialects are often refered to as a “heavy-light” pattern (Ballard, 1989: 105). More specifically, at the word/compound level, the stress is assigned leftmostly (Chen, 2000: 309).
